narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'sits not in the seat of scoffers', read as a volition (type 102): an act the will settles, not an affect that arrives. The bearer (105) is the blessed man, and the operation (106) is the third and deepest of three refusals - he does not sit in the seat of scoffers, declining the settled fellowship of scorn - with its target (107) marked 'refusal-3', the climax of a descent the interior turns down. The coupling (112) 'sit-not' binds the verb to its own negation: the finding is the refusal itself, the will's fixed No to belonging. No source is recorded (103 absent) - the passage names nothing that provokes or pushes the refusal; it stands as free, un-triggered volition. No organ seats it (104 none): this is a whole-self posture, not lodged in heart or eyes. Manner is unmarked (108 none), and intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are all unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent) - the verse grades no degree, adds no qualifier, names no in-verse result, and frames no command; it simply shows the will's settled refusal. The discovery (114) reads the triad walk->stand->sit as the whole slide the interior declines, sitting being permanent belonging and scoffers the most corrosive company. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116). In a family otherwise built on defiance against God, this reading is the inverse pole - here rebellion is the very thing refused, and the wicked/sinners/scoffers are the arena the inner life turns from.
narratives.story: The psalm opens by praising a man for what he will not do. He will not walk along with the wicked, will not stop and stand where sinners gather, and - deepest of all - will not sit down and settle among those who mock. Sitting means belonging, and he refuses to belong there; it is a firm choice of the will, a settled inner No, not something forced on him. The psalm names nothing that tempts him and promises no reward in the moment - it simply shows which way his inner life leans: away from the company of scorn. In a group of passages otherwise full of defiance against God, this one stands apart, because here it is defiance itself that is being turned down.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is that the enemies have rebelled, read as a volition (type 102) - a set of the will, not merely a deed. The bearer (105) is the enemies, and the operation (106) is that they have rebelled against God, so the self asks God to let them fall by their own counsels: revolt is diagnosed as their bent. The target (107) is 'rebellion' itself and the coupling (112) 'rebelled-against-God' fixes the direction of the revolt Godward. No source is recorded (103 absent) - no cause or trigger is assigned; the rebellion stands as their own inward orientation. No organ seats it (104 none): it is a whole-self direction, not lodged in an organ. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent) - the verse grades no degree, adds no qualifier, names no in-verse consequence, frames no command. The discovery (114) is the finding: beneath the enemies' deceit toward the psalmist lies a deeper diagnosis - their interior is set against God himself, so their treachery to the man is really revolt against God. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116). The lens stays on the enemies' inner orientation, with God as the arena their revolt is aimed at.
narratives.story: Surrounded by treacherous enemies, the psalmist asks God to let them collapse under their own schemes, and he names why: they have rebelled against God. The point is not just their lies against him but what those lies expose - an inner life set in opposition to God. Their deceit toward a man turns out to be, at root, revolt against God. The psalm does not explain what made them this way or measure how far their rebellion goes; it simply reads their treachery as the surface of a deeper defiance. What we see is an interior bent against God, betraying itself in how it treats others.
narratives.variation_note: This item (H4784:rebell) has five readings. Here (#1) the bearer is the psalmist's enemies and the type is volition - rebellion diagnosed as the settled Godward bent beneath their deceit. In the four wilderness readings (#2 78:17, #3 78:40, #4 106:7, #5 107:11) the same marah is typed as action and the bearer is Israel's own fathers rebelling against God in the desert or against his words. The shift in bearer (outside enemies vs. the covenant people) and type (volition vs. repeated action) is the finding: one word names both the outsider's fixed hostility and the insider's recurring defiance.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'why have you forsaken me', read as affect (type 102): this forsakenness is felt, an emotional condition, not a chosen act. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, and the operation (106) is the self's cry that God has forsaken it and is far from saving, far from the words of its groaning - the extremity of felt abandonment. The target (107) is 'forsakenness' and the coupling (112) 'why-forsaken' binds the movement to its own unanswered question. No source is recorded (103 absent) - and here the silence is itself the wound: no cause for the abandonment is given, and the sufferer cannot name why. No organ seats it (104 none): the desolation fills the whole self rather than lodging in a named seat. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent) - the cry is neither graded, subtyped, given an in-verse resolution, nor framed as command; it is left raw and open. The discovery (114) sharpens the finding: this is the interior's rawest desolation - not doubt that God exists but the agony of his felt absence. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116). God is the one the cry is flung toward, the arena; the movement is the inner life's collapse into felt abandonment.
narratives.story: The psalmist cries out to God with the hardest question there is: why have you left me? He feels utterly abandoned - God seems far off, deaf to his groaning, out of reach of any rescue. This is not doubt about whether God is real; it is the raw pain of God's felt absence. The psalm gives no reason for the abandonment and offers no comfort in the moment - the sufferer cannot even say why it has come, and no answer is supplied. What we see is a whole self sinking into the agony of feeling forsaken by the one it still calls 'my God'.
narratives.variation_note: This item (H5800:forsaken) has three readings. Here (#1) forsakenness is an affect suffered - God's felt abandonment of the psalmist. In #2 (27:10) it is again affect but the forsakers are father and mother, and the movement resolves upward into trust (the LORD takes me in). In #3 (119:87) it becomes a disposition and is negated - the psalmist has NOT forsaken God's precepts though nearly destroyed. Across the three the bearer and direction invert: from being forsaken (by God-felt, by parents) to refusing to forsake.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'I am a worm, not a man', read as a state (type 102): a condition of the self, not an act or a passing feeling. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, and the operation (106) is that he reckons himself a worm and not a man, scorned and despised by all - a self-estimate crushed below humanity. The target (107) is 'self-abasement' and the coupling (112) 'worm-not-man' binds the self-reckoning to its own degradation. No source is recorded (103 absent) - though mockery presses from every side, the field assigns no cause; the state simply stands. No organ seats it (104 none): the collapse is a whole-self condition, not seated in a named organ. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent) - the abasement is not graded, subtyped, given an in-verse outcome, or commanded. The discovery (114) reads it as a collapse of self-worth: mockery has driven the interior below the human. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116). Mankind and the people are the arena whose scorn presses in, but the reading is of the interior's own reckoning sinking beneath manhood.
narratives.story: Battered by contempt, the psalmist looks at himself and sees not a man but a worm - despised, mocked, treated as less than human. This is not a mood that comes and goes but a settled sense of who he now is: his worth has caved in under the scorn of others. The psalm does not spell out exactly what did this or how far it goes; it simply lets the crushed self-estimate stand. The scorn of the crowd is the pressure, but what we actually see is a person whose inner sense of himself has sunk below being human at all.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'though parents forsake, God takes me in', read as affect (type 102) - a felt orientation, not a deliberate act. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, and the operation (106) is that even if father and mother forsake it, the self is confident the LORD will take it up: security reaching beyond the closest human bonds. The target (107) is 'abandonment-answered' and the coupling (112) 'God-takes-me-in' binds the felt abandonment to its resolution. No source is recorded (103 absent) - the psalm does not trace where this confidence comes from, only that it holds when parents fail. No organ seats it (104 none): the security is a whole-self stance, not organ-lodged. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent) - no degree, no qualifier, no in-verse outcome beyond the assurance, no command. The discovery (114) reads it as trust that outlasts the failure of the deepest human belonging: the interior rests where even parents cannot be relied on. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116). Parents are the arena whose forsaking is imagined; the movement is the inner life anchored in God past that loss.
narratives.story: The psalmist imagines the most painful abandonment of all - even a father and mother turning away - and answers it with quiet confidence: the LORD will take me in. The felt loss is real, but it is met and overtaken by a deeper security. The psalm does not explain where this confidence comes from or how strongly it is held; it simply rests there, unshaken by the worst human failure. What we see is an inner life that has found a footing beyond even the closest family bonds.
narratives.variation_note: This item (H5800:forsaken) has three readings. Here (#2) forsakenness is an affect, but the forsakers are father and mother and the movement resolves into trust that God receives the abandoned self. In #1 (22:1) it is the felt abandonment by God himself, left raw and unanswered. In #3 (119:87) it is a disposition, negated - the psalmist has not forsaken God's precepts. The same word swings from being forsaken by God, to being forsaken by parents yet held, to refusing to forsake God: bearer and direction shift each time.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'refrain from anger, forsake wrath', read as a volition (type 102): an act the will must perform, not a feeling that simply comes. The bearer (105) is the hearer being addressed, and the operation (106) is the deliberate release of anger - the self is told to let go of anger and forsake wrath, for fretting tends only to evil. The target (107) is 'anger-release' and the coupling (112) 'refrain-from-anger' binds the command to its object. No source is recorded (103 absent) - the verse does not trace where the anger arose; it addresses only its letting-go. No organ seats it (104 none): the release is a whole-self act, not lodged in a named seat. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent) - though the verse warns that fretting 'tends only to evil', the effect field itself is empty, and no degree, qualifier, or formal command-prohibition is marked. The discovery (114) reads it as the letting-go of anger, the interior warned that nursed wrath breeds only harm. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116). This reading, like the refusals in the family, is a turning-from - here the inner life is urged to release its own anger before it curdles into evil.
narratives.story: The psalm urges the listener to let go of anger and put wrath aside, warning that stewing over things leads only to harm. This is presented as something to choose and do, not a feeling to wait out: deliberately release the anger. The verse does not say what stirred the anger in the first place; it cares only about setting it down. And though it warns that brooding does damage, its whole weight falls on the act of letting go. What we see is an inner life being coached to release its own resentment before it turns into something worse.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'leave / abandon' (azab - wealth to others), read as an action (type 102) rather than a state or affect. The bearer (105) is the dying, wise and fool alike, and the operation (106) is to leave behind, its target (107) their wealth, passed to others. Here the coupling is explicitly 'none' (112, resolution none): no companion movement is welded to it - the leaving stands bare and solitary, which fits its meaning, since death strips a person of every tie to what they held. No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse does not trace a cause beyond the plain fact of dying. No organ seats it (104 none): it is not an organ's act but the whole person's forced release at death. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent) - no degree, qualifier, in-verse outcome, or command. The discovery (114) reads it as the futility of hoarding: azab here is the forced abandonment of wealth at death, the riches passing to strangers, possessions that cannot follow. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116). Uniquely in this family the target is not God or law but wealth - 'forsaking' turned outward onto possessions; the inner-being finding is the interior's confrontation with the emptiness of what it cannot keep.
narratives.story: The psalm observes a hard fact: wise and foolish alike must die, and when they do they leave their wealth to others. The word for it is the same one used elsewhere for forsaking or abandoning - here it is the forced letting-go of everything a person hoarded, handed off to strangers who did not earn it. Nothing is welded to this leaving; it stands alone and stark, as death does. The psalm does not dress it up or soften it. What we see is the inner life brought face to face with the emptiness of piling up things that cannot follow it past the grave.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'let not the rebellious exalt themselves' (sarar), read as a status (type 102): a settled condition of the person, not a single deed. Unusually for this family, a source IS recorded (103, a span pair): the rebellious are 'watched by God's eyes on the nations' - their defiance is set under God's surveillance, the origin-context that hems it in. The bearer (105) is the rebellious, and the operation (106), also a span pair, is 'exalt themselves' - the self-lifting God's watching eyes restrain. The target (107) is 'none' (resolution none): the self-exaltation is aimed at no named object beyond the self - it curves back on itself, self-referential pride. The coupling (112, pair) binds the rebellious to their self-exalting. No organ seats it (104 none). Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent) - the verse neither grades nor forbids in a formal sense, though the jussive 'let not' hovers over it. The discovery (114) reads it as the defiant whom God's watching eyes restrain, warned not to lift themselves against the God who rules the nations. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116). The presence of a source here - divine watching - is itself the finding: this rebellion is defined by the God who oversees it.
narratives.story: As the psalm celebrates God's rule over the nations, it adds a warning: let the rebellious not lift themselves up. What marks these defiant ones is that God's eyes are on them - their revolt takes place under his constant watch, and that is what hems it in. Their self-exaltation has no real object outside themselves; it is pride curving back on itself. The psalm does not measure their defiance or spell out a punishment; it simply sets them under the gaze of the God who rules everything. What we see is a rebellious inner life warned not to raise itself against the One who is watching.
narratives.variation_note: This item (H5637:rebelliou, sarar) has three readings, all typed as status. Here (#1) a source is present - God's watching eyes on the nations - and the operation is self-exaltation restrained. In #2 (68:6) the operation is dwelling in a parched land, a scorched exile marked as their manner - rebellion's consequence. In #3 (68:18) the astonishing turn: God receives gifts and dwells even among the rebellious - grace reaching the defiant. Across the three the same word moves restraint -> judgment -> grace: how the rebellious are handled shifts entirely with context.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'the rebellious dwell in a parched land' (sarar), read as a status (type 102): a settled condition, not a single act. The bearer (105) is the rebellious, and the operation (106) is to dwell in a parched land - here the movement is not their defiance directly but its outcome-place. The manner (108) is marked and load-bearing: 'in a sun-scorched land' - the one graded qualifier in the reading, coloring their dwelling as barren exile. The target (107) is 'none' (resolution none): the dwelling is aimed at no object; it is simply where rebellion lands. The coupling (112, span pair) is the finding: the rebellious are set against 'the solitary God settles in a home and the prisoners he leads out to prosperity' - their scorched homelessness is the deliberate foil to God's home-giving. No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse does not trace the origin of their rebellion, only its reward. No organ seats it (104 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the defiant left in barren exile - rebellion's reward a scorched, homeless waste. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116). God is the arena whose home-giving they are contrasted against; the inner-being reading is of an orientation that ends outside the shelter God gives.
narratives.story: The psalm pictures God as one who gives the lonely a home and leads prisoners out into freedom - and then sets the rebellious against that picture: they are left to live in a parched, sun-scorched land. Their defiance does not get its own dramatic scene here; instead we see where it ends up - a barren, homeless waste. That dry exile is the exact opposite of the homes God provides for others. The psalm does not say how their rebellion began, only how it turns out. What we see is a defiant inner life that ends up shut out of the shelter God freely gives.
narratives.variation_note: This item (H5637:rebelliou, sarar) has three readings, all status. Here (#2) the operation is dwelling in a scorched land - rebellion's barren consequence, uniquely carrying a marked manner ('sun-scorched'), and paired as the foil to God's home-giving. In #1 (66:7) the rebellious are under God's watching eyes and restrained from self-exaltation. In #3 (68:18) God dwells even among them - grace. The same word moves restraint -> judgment (here) -> grace across the set.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'even among the rebellious, that God may dwell' (sarar), read as a status (type 102): a settled condition of the person. The bearer (105) is the rebellious, and the operation (106) is that they receive gifts - even they - so that the LORD God may dwell there. The target (107) is 'none' (resolution none): no object is aimed at; the reading is not about an act the rebellious perform but about what is done toward them. The coupling (112, span pair) is the finding: 'the rebellious among whom God nonetheless dwells' - defiance is the very company grace penetrates. No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse does not trace the origin of their rebellion. No organ seats it (104 none). Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as grace reaching even the defiant - the marvel that the ascended God's victory-gifts extend even to former enemies, that he chooses to dwell among rebels. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116). Here the inner-being lens is turned inside out: the rebellious interior is not acting but being acted upon by grace - God is the arena, but the movement runs from God toward the defiant.
narratives.story: Celebrating God's triumphant ascent, the psalm says something startling: he receives gifts and takes up residence even among the rebellious. The defiant do nothing to earn this; the wonder is entirely on God's side, that he would give and dwell among those who resisted him. Rebellion here is not a scene of revolt but the very crowd that grace reaches into. The psalm does not explain how these people became rebellious or measure their defiance; it marvels only that God comes to them anyway. What we see is a defiant inner life that becomes, against all expectation, the place God chooses to live.
narratives.variation_note: This item (H5637:rebelliou, sarar) has three readings, all status. Here (#3) the movement runs from God toward the rebellious - grace, gifts, and God dwelling even among the defiant; the rebellious are acted upon, not acting. In #1 (66:7) they are restrained under God's watching eyes; in #2 (68:6) they are left in a scorched land - judgment. The same word carries restraint, judgment, and grace across the three, the sharpest swing in the family.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'is the enemy to revile your name forever?' (naats), read as an action (type 102): an active contempt, not a state. The bearer (105) is the enemy, and the operation (106) is to revile / spurn. The target (107) is a span pair - 'God's name, forever' - the finding that the contempt is aimed squarely at the divine name itself. The manner (108) is marked, 'forever', giving the reviling a duration that intensifies the outrage. The coupling (112, span pair) binds it with the enemy's scoffing - reviling and scoffing move together. No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse does not trace what drives the enemy's contempt; it stands as their act. No organ seats it (104 none): it is a whole-self act of the foe, not organ-lodged. Intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent) - no degree beyond 'forever', no qualifier, no in-verse outcome, no command. The discovery (114) reads it as the contempt of God's name the psalmist cannot bear: naats here is the spurning of God's very name by the foe, blasphemy that God is implored to answer, the enemy's insult to God the heart of the crisis. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116). God is the arena the contempt strikes at; the reading exposes the enemy's interior turned to open scorn of the divine name.
narratives.story: Standing amid a ruined sanctuary, the psalmist's deepest anguish is not the wreckage but the enemy's mockery of God's very name - and the dread that it will go on forever. The foe's contempt is active and aimed straight at God, spat out alongside their scoffing. The psalm does not explain what makes the enemy so contemptuous; it simply shows the insult and begs God to answer it. What cuts most is that God himself is being reviled. What we see is a hostile inner life pouring open scorn on God's name, and a worshipper who cannot bear that it should last.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'my soul refuses to be comforted' (maen), read as a disposition (type 102): a settled inward set, not a one-off act. Uniquely in this family a seat IS named (104, a span pair): 'the soul (nephesh)' - the refusal is lodged in the deep self, the only reading here that locates the movement in a named organ of the inner being. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, and the operation (106) is to refuse / decline. The target (107, span pair) is 'comfort' - what the soul turns away from. The manner (108) is marked, 'resolute inconsolability' - a firmness that measures the depth of the grief. The coupling (112, span pair) binds the soul and the comfort refused. No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse does not name the specific trouble's origin, only that it is 'the day of my trouble'. Intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the active turning-away from consolation: grief so deep it declines to be eased, a refusal that measures the weight of the distress. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116). Here refusal is turned not against God or law but against comfort itself - the inner being's grief refusing to be soothed, God being the one sought even as consolation is declined.
narratives.story: In deep trouble, reaching out to God through the night, the psalmist finds his very soul refusing to be comforted. This is not a passing mood but a settled inner set, planted deep in him: he turns away even from consolation. That firm refusal is itself a measure of how heavy his grief is - it is too deep to be talked out of. The psalm does not name exactly what caused the trouble; it only shows the soul declining to be soothed. What we see is an inner life so weighed down that it pushes comfort away, even while it keeps crying out to God.
narratives.variation_note: This item (H3985:refus, maen) has two readings. Here (#1) the refusal is a disposition, uniquely seated in the soul (nephesh), aimed at comfort - inward grief declining consolation, with God still sought. In #2 (78:10) it is an action, no seat, aimed at God's law - the fathers' willed rejection of obedience, defiance turned Godward. The same verb swings from grief refusing comfort (inward, sorrowful) to the will refusing to obey (outward, defiant); the seat appears only where the refusal is grief.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'we will not hide them from their children' (kachad), read as an action (type 102). The bearer (105) is 'we', the transmitting generation, and the operation (106) is to refuse to conceal - a negated hiding, which is the reading's hinge: the characteristic is a refusal-to-withhold. The target (107) is 'God's deeds from the children' - what is deliberately not hidden. The coupling (112) binds it with the resolve to tell: not-hiding and telling are one motion. No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse does not trace the impulse behind the resolve. No organ seats it (104 none): it is a whole-self commitment, not organ-lodged. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent) - no degree, qualifier, in-verse outcome, or command. Distinctively, the locus (116) is 'external:person' - the only reading in the family whose orientation runs outward toward other people (the children, the coming generation) rather than into the ib-state. The discovery (114) reads it as the resolve NOT to conceal God's deeds from the young, transmission as duty. Role is characteristic (115). Here the family's typical 'refusing' turns constructive: the inner life sets itself against concealment, and its arena is the next generation who must be told.
narratives.story: The psalmist and his generation make a firm resolve: they will not keep God's mighty deeds hidden from their children, but will pass them on to the generation still to come. The characteristic here is a refusal - but a good one, a refusal to hold back the story. Not-hiding and telling are the same single act. The psalm does not explain what moved them to it; it simply shows the commitment, and it points outward, toward the young who must hear. What we see is an inner life deliberately set against secrecy, aimed at handing the truth forward to the next generation.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'refused to walk according to his law' (maen), read as an action (type 102): an active rejection, not a passing mood. The bearer (105) is the fathers, and the operation (106) is to refuse. The target (107) is 'to walk according to his law' - obedience itself is what is declined. The coupling (112) binds it with the covenant unkept: the refusal and the broken covenant move together. No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse does not trace what produced the refusal, only that it stood. No organ seats it (104 none): it is a whole-will act, not organ-lodged. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent). The locus (116) is 'external:god' - the refusal is oriented Godward, aimed at his law. The discovery (114) reads it plainly as the willed rejection of obedience. Role is characteristic (115). Here the same verb that elsewhere marks grief refusing comfort marks the will refusing God: the inner being's deliberate No to walking in God's law, with God as the arena it defies.
narratives.story: Recalling Israel's fathers, the psalm charges them with refusing to live by God's law. This was not weakness or forgetfulness but an active choice to say No to obedience, bound up with their failure to keep the covenant. The psalm does not explain what made them refuse; it simply records that they did, and that their refusal was aimed straight at God's commands. What we see is an inner life deliberately turning down the path God set - a will set against him.
narratives.variation_note: This item (H3985:refus, maen) has two readings. Here (#2) the refusal is an action aimed at God's law - the fathers' willed rejection of obedience, oriented Godward, with no seat named. In #1 (77:2) it is a disposition seated in the soul, aimed at comfort - grief declining consolation. The same verb divides sharply: inward, sorrowful refusal of comfort versus outward, defiant refusal to obey.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be rebellious' (marah), read as a status (type 102): the ingrained condition of a generation, not a single deed. The bearer (105) is the fathers, and the operation (106) is to rebel / defy, its target (107) 'God'. The coupling (112) binds it with stubbornness: rebelliousness and obstinacy are welded as twin marks of the same generation, standing beside 'a heart not steadfast, a spirit not faithful'. No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse does not trace where the defiance came from - it is presented as a settled trait, warned against as an inheritance. No organ seats it (104 none): it is a whole-generation condition, not organ-lodged, though the surrounding verse speaks of an unsteady heart and faithless spirit. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the ingrained defiance that marked the wilderness fathers - the very trait the young are urged not to inherit. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116). God is the arena the defiance faces; the reading holds up rebelliousness as a settled interior condition passed down a family line.
narratives.story: The psalm warns the young not to become like their fathers - a stubborn and rebellious generation, their hearts never steady, their spirit never faithful to God. Rebelliousness here is not one bad act but a settled trait, an ingrained defiance that ran through that whole generation, tied tightly to their stubbornness. The psalm does not say how it first took hold; it simply names it as a condition and warns against passing it on. What we see is a defiant inner disposition treated almost as an inheritance - something a new generation is urged not to receive.
narratives.variation_note: This item (H4784:rebelliou, marah) has two readings. Here (#1) it is a status - the settled, inherited condition of the wilderness generation, paired with stubbornness and warned against. In #2 (106:43) it is a disposition - a recurring bent shown across cycles of deliverance and relapse. Status (a fixed condition to avoid inheriting) versus disposition (a repeating tendency exposed over time): the difference marks whether rebellion is being defined as a state or traced as a pattern.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be stubborn' (sarar), read as a status (type 102): a settled obstinacy, not a single act. The bearer (105) is the fathers, and the operation (106) is to be obstinate, its target (107) 'against God'. The coupling (112) binds it with rebelliousness and the unsteady heart - the finding is that stubbornness stands beside, but distinct from, the rebelliousness (marah) in the same verse. Directive to preserve distinctions applies here: this passage holds two separate lexicals in one line - stubborn (sarar) names the immovable obstinacy, rebellious (marah) names the active defiance; they are welded but not identical, and the difference is the finding. No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse does not trace the origin of the obstinacy. No organ seats it (104 none), though the surrounding line names a heart not steadfast. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the obstinacy the young are warned not to inherit. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116). God is the arena the obstinacy is set against; the reading isolates the immovable, dug-in quality of the inner life that will not be turned.
narratives.story: In the same warning, the psalm names a second fault beside rebelliousness: stubbornness. Where rebellion is active defiance, stubbornness is the dug-in, immovable quality of a heart that simply will not be turned - and the psalm keeps the two distinct even though they sit side by side. This obstinacy was a settled trait of the fathers, set against God, and the young are warned not to take it on. The psalm does not explain how it formed; it simply names it as a condition. What we see is an inner life that has hardened into a refusal to budge, held up as a trait to avoid inheriting.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'rebel' (marah), read as an action (type 102): an active deed of defiance. The bearer (105) is 'they', the wilderness generation, and the operation (106) is to rebel, its target (107) 'against the Most High'. The coupling (112) binds it with the sinning - 'they sinned still more against him, rebelling' - so defiance and mounting sin move together. No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse does not trace a cause; the defiance is their own act, all the starker for coming amid God's provision. No organ seats it (104 none), though the surrounding verses expose their heart demanding food and their speaking against God. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent) - no degree, qualifier, in-verse outcome, or command. The discovery (114) reads it as defiance in the very place of God's provision: rebelling against the Most High in the desert. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is 'external:god' - the rebellion is oriented Godward. God, who has just been shown providing, is the arena the defiance strikes at; the reading exposes an inner life that heaps rebellion onto sin in the wilderness.
narratives.story: Even after all God had done, the people kept sinning against him, rebelling against the Most High out in the desert. Their defiance was an active thing, piling onto sin already committed, and it happened in the very place where God was providing for them. The psalm does not offer an excuse or a cause; it simply shows them turning against God where he had been most present to help. What we see is an inner life that answers provision with revolt, adding rebellion to sin in the wilderness.
narratives.variation_note: One of five readings of H4784:rebell. Here (#2) marah is an action, bearer 'they' (the wilderness generation), rebelling against the Most High in the desert, coupled with escalating sin. It differs from #1 (5:10, the enemies' Godward bent, typed volition) in bearer and type, and from #3/#4/#5 in its specific pairing (with sinning, versus grieving God in #3, failure to remember in #4, spurning his counsel in #5): the repeated verb is anchored each time to a different companion movement, mapping how one defiance recurs across the wilderness story.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'rebel' (marah), read as an action (type 102). The bearer (105) is 'they', and the operation (106) is to rebel, its target (107) 'against God in the wilderness'. The coupling (112) binds it with grieving him - 'how often they rebelled against him and grieved him' - so the defiance is welded to the pain it caused God. No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse traces no cause but frames the rebellion with 'how often', marking it as wearyingly repeated. No organ seats it (104 none), though the surrounding line recalls that 'their heart was not steadfast'. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent) - the repetition ('how often') is carried in the operation, not graded as intensity. The discovery (114) reads it as the recurring, wearying defiance. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is 'external:god'. God, shown here as compassionate and restraining his anger, is the arena the defiance grieves; the reading exposes an inner life whose repeated rebellion wounds the very God who keeps sparing it.
narratives.story: The psalm marvels, sadly, at how often the people rebelled against God in the wilderness and grieved him - and it comes right after describing God as compassionate, holding back his anger, remembering they were only frail flesh. Their defiance was not a single lapse but a wearying, repeated thing, and it caused God real grief. The psalm gives no reason for it; it simply counts how often it happened. What we see is an inner life that keeps turning against a God who keeps forgiving it, wounding the very one who spares it.
narratives.variation_note: One of five readings of H4784:rebell. Here (#3) marah is an action, coupled specifically with grieving God, and framed by 'how often' - the repeated, wearying defiance set against God's compassion. It differs from #1 (5:10, enemies, volition) and from #2/#4/#5 in its companion pairing (grieving him, versus sinning in #2, failure to remember in #4, spurning counsel in #5). The same verb is repeatedly re-anchored, tracking how one recurring defiance wears against divine patience.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'rebel' (marah), read as an action (type 102). The bearer (105) is 'they', now settled in the land, and the operation (106) is to rebel, its target (107) 'against the Most High'. The coupling (112) binds it with the testing - 'they tested and rebelled against the Most High God' - so trial-by-doubt and defiance move together. No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse traces no cause, which sharpens the finding, since this defiance comes after full deliverance and settlement. No organ seats it (104 none), though the surrounding lines expose a 'deceitful bow' and idolatrous high places. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as defiance persisting into settled possession - rebellion that outlives the wilderness and continues in the promised land. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is 'external:god'. God, who has just given them the land and driven out nations before them, is the arena the defiance strikes at; the reading exposes an inner orientation that carries rebellion even into the place of fulfilled promise.
narratives.story: Even after God brought them into the promised land and settled them there, the people tested and rebelled against him again, refusing to keep his commands. Their defiance did not end with the wilderness; it followed them into the very home God had won for them, tangled up with doubt and later with idolatry. The psalm offers no cause for it - it simply shows rebellion outliving every rescue and every gift. What we see is an inner life that carries its defiance even into the place where every promise had been kept.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'stubborn' (sheriruth), read as a status (type 102): a settled obstinacy of the inner life. The bearer (105) is 'my people', and the operation (106) is to be stubborn, its target (107) 'in heart' - the obstinacy is located in the heart even though no organ is formally seated. The coupling (112) binds it with 'their own counsels': God gives them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own devices - obstinacy and self-will move together. No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse does not trace where the stubbornness came from, only that God finally handed them to it. No organ seats it (104 none) at the formal level, though the target names 'in heart'. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the obstinacy God finally left them to - judgment by abandonment: 'I gave them over to their stubborn hearts'. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116). Distinct from the sarar stubbornness of 78:8 (warned against as an inheritance), this sheriruth stubbornness is the very thing God surrenders them to - the inner life's obstinacy becomes its own punishment when God stops resisting it. God is the arena: his people would not submit, and he responds by releasing them to their own hardness.
narratives.story: God recalls that his people would not listen or submit to him - so he gave them up to their own stubborn hearts, letting them follow their own devices. The terrible thing here is that their obstinacy became its own sentence: God simply stopped holding them back and let their hardened hearts have their way. The stubbornness is set deep in the heart, bound up with their determination to run their own counsel. The psalm does not say how their hearts got so hard; it shows God handing them over to it as judgment. What we see is an inner life so set against God that being left to itself is the punishment.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'forsake' (azab), read as an action (type 102). The bearer (105) is 'David's children', and the operation (106) is to forsake, its target (107) 'God's law'. The coupling (112) binds it with 'not walking in his rules': forsaking the law and abandoning obedience are one movement. The reading sits inside a covenant conditional - 'if his children forsake my law' - so this is a hypothetical, projected defiance held within God's larger promise never to remove his steadfast love. No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse does not trace a cause; it names the possibility, not its origin. No organ seats it (104 none): it is a whole-will act, not organ-lodged. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent) - though the surrounding verses promise the rod for such transgression, the effect field itself is empty. The discovery (114) reads it as the apostasy of the sons, abandonment of God's covenant word. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is 'external:god'. God is the arena the forsaking is aimed at; the reading holds up covenant-abandonment as a possibility built into the promise itself, defiance anticipated and answered by discipline rather than by withdrawal of love.
narratives.story: In the covenant with David, God allows for the possibility that David's own descendants might forsake his law and stop walking in his ways. If they do, he says, he will discipline them - but he will never take back his steadfast love. Here forsaking means abandoning God's commands, an act of the will, spoken of as something that might happen rather than something already done. The psalm does not explain what would drive such abandonment; it simply builds the possibility into the promise. What we see is covenant-abandonment anticipated in advance - a defiance God is ready to meet with correction, not with the end of his faithfulness.
narratives.variation_note: This item (H5800:forsak, azab) has two readings. Here (#1) the bearer is David's own children (covenant heirs) and the forsaking is hypothetical - a conditional 'if they forsake my law', held within God's promise of enduring love. In #2 (119:53) the bearer is the wicked and the forsaking is an actual, present reality that fires the psalmist's indignation. The difference is bearer (covenant sons vs. the wicked) and mode (a projected possibility inside covenant fidelity vs. a real defiance provoking zeal).

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fall away' (set), read as a status (type 102): a condition of the turned-aside, not a single act. The bearer (105) is 'the crooked', and the operation (106) is to fall away / turn aside, its target (107) 'from God's way'. The reading's coupling and locus fields carry each other's content (the coupling field holds 'internal:ib-state' and the locus field holds 'paired with the hated work'); read together, the movement is an interior state (116, internal:ib-state) welded to the hated work of the apostates (112). No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse does not trace what caused the turning-aside. No organ seats it (104 none): it is a whole-self defection, not organ-lodged. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the turncoats whose deeds David hates - the apostates he will not let cling to him. Role is characteristic (115). Here the family's defiance appears from the vantage of the one refusing it: David hates the work of those who fall away and resolves it shall not cling to him. The falling-away is the interior state of the crooked; the arena is God's way, from which they have turned - and against which David sets his own integrity of heart.
narratives.story: In a psalm about keeping his own life clean, David declares that he hates the deeds of those who fall away from God's path, and he will not let such things cling to him. The people in view are the crooked, whose whole bent has turned aside from God's way - a settled condition of defection, not a single slip. The psalm does not explain how they came to fall away; it simply names them and David's refusal to let their ways stick to him. What we see is one man's determined integrity set against the turned-aside inner life of others - defiance viewed from the side of the one rejecting it.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'rebel' (marah, negated), read as a disposition (type 102): here the characteristic appears as its absence - a not-rebelling. The bearer (105) is 'Moses and Aaron', and the operation (106) is to NOT rebel, its target (107) 'against God's words'. The reading's coupling and locus fields carry each other's content (the coupling field holds 'external:god' and the locus field holds 'paired with performing the signs'); read together, the movement is oriented Godward (116, external:god) and welded to their faithful performing of his signs (112). No source is recorded (103 absent). No organ seats it (104 none): it is a whole-will fidelity, not organ-lodged. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the obedience of Moses and Aaron - faithful agents who did not resist God's commission. Role is characteristic (115). This is the family's key negative-space reading: against a book of rebellion, here the defiance is precisely what does NOT occur. Silence is evidence - the absence of rebellion is itself the finding, marking Moses and Aaron as the counter-image to the wilderness generation: sent by God, they carried out his word without resistance. God is the arena; their inner life bends to his commission rather than against it.
narratives.story: As the psalm retells the plagues in Egypt, it pauses to note something about Moses and Aaron: they did not rebel against God's words. In a story otherwise full of defiance, here defiance is exactly what is missing. Sent by God to perform his signs, these two carried out his commission faithfully, without resisting. The psalm does not explain their obedience; it simply marks its presence by naming the rebellion that did not happen. What we see is an inner life that bends to God's word instead of against it - the bright counter-image to a rebellious generation.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'rebel' (marah), read as an action (type 102). The bearer (105) is 'the fathers', and the operation (106) is to rebel, its target (107) 'against God at the sea'. The reading's coupling and locus fields carry each other's content (the coupling field holds 'external:god' and the locus field holds 'paired with the failure to remember'); read together, the rebellion is Godward (116, external:god) and welded to their failure to remember his steadfast love (112). No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse traces no cause but sets the defiance beside a failure of memory - they 'did not consider his wondrous works... but rebelled'. No organ seats it (104 none). Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the first act of the confession's catalogue: defiance at the very edge of deliverance, 'at the Red Sea'. Role is characteristic (115). This reading opens Psalm 106's long confession of national rebellion; the finding is that defiance stands at the threshold of rescue, coupled to forgetfulness. God, in the very act of delivering, is the arena the rebellion strikes at; the inner life fails to remember and so revolts on the brink of salvation.
narratives.story: Confessing the nation's long history of sin, the psalm names its first act: at the Red Sea, on the very edge of being rescued, the fathers rebelled against God. Their defiance was bound up with forgetfulness - they failed to take in his wonders and his steadfast love, and so they revolted right where he was saving them. The psalm does not excuse it; it lays it down as the opening entry in a catalogue of rebellion. What we see is an inner life that forgets what God has done and turns against him at the threshold of deliverance.
narratives.variation_note: One of five readings of H4784:rebell. Here (#4) marah is an action, bearer 'the fathers', rebelling against God at the Red Sea, coupled with the failure to remember his love. It differs from #1 (5:10, enemies, volition) and from #2/#3/#5 in its companion pairing (forgetfulness, versus sinning in #2, grieving God in #3, spurning counsel in #5). Each recurrence re-anchors the same verb to a new adjoining movement, charting how one defiance repeats through the confession.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'despise' (maas), read as an action (type 102): active contempt, not a passing state. The bearer (105) is 'the fathers', and the operation (106) is to despise, its target (107) 'the pleasant land'. The reading's coupling and locus fields carry each other's content (the coupling field holds 'internal:ib-state' and the locus field holds 'paired with having no faith'); read together, the contempt is an interior state (116, internal:ib-state) welded to their having no faith in God's promise (112). No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse traces no cause, though it sits amid a chain of unbelief and murmuring. No organ seats it (104 none): it is a whole-self scorn, not organ-lodged. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the scorn of Canaan at Kadesh - rejecting God's gift, refusing the pleasant land in unbelief. Role is characteristic (115). Distinct from the enemy's reviling of God's name (naats, 74:10) and the psalmist's own despised estate (bazah, 119:141), this maas contempt is aimed at God's gift: the inner life scorns the very land God promised, its unbelief curdling into disdain. God is the arena - to despise his gift is to despise him.
narratives.story: Recalling the wilderness, the psalm charges the fathers with despising the pleasant land - the good country God had promised them. This was active scorn, not mere hesitation: they had no faith in God's promise, and their unbelief soured into contempt for his gift. To reject the land was, in effect, to reject God himself. The psalm does not explain what hardened them; it simply names the disdain and the faithlessness behind it. What we see is an inner life that looks at God's best gift and turns up its nose, unbelief hardening into scorn.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'rebellious' (marah), read as a disposition (type 102): a recurring bent, not a single act. The bearer (105) is 'the fathers', and the operation (106) is to be rebellious, its target (107) 'in their purposes'. The reading's coupling and locus fields carry each other's content (the coupling field holds 'external:god' and the locus field holds 'paired with their self-willed counsel'); read together, the rebelliousness is Godward (116, external:god) and welded to their own self-willed counsel (112). No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse traces no cause but frames the defiance inside a cycle - 'many times he delivered them, but they were rebellious'. No organ seats it (104 none). Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as persistent defiance: deliverance met again with rebellion, and the people 'brought low through their iniquity'. Role is characteristic (115). The finding is the cycle itself - repeated rescue answered by repeated rebellion, the inner life so bent on its own purposes that even deliverance cannot turn it. God, delivering many times over, is the arena the disposition keeps defying.
narratives.story: The psalm describes a wearying pattern: again and again God rescued his people, and again and again they were rebellious in their own plans, dragged down by their sin. Rebelliousness here is a settled bent, a tendency that kept reasserting itself no matter how often they were saved. They were set on following their own counsel, and even repeated deliverance could not turn them. The psalm does not explain the root of it; it simply lays bare the cycle. What we see is an inner life so fixed on its own way that God's mercy, offered over and over, keeps meeting the same defiance.
narratives.variation_note: This item (H4784:rebelliou, marah) has two readings. Here (#2) it is a disposition - a recurring bent exposed across cycles of deliverance and relapse, bound to their self-willed counsel. In #1 (78:8) it is a status - the fixed, inherited condition of the wilderness generation, warned against and paired with stubbornness. Disposition (a repeating tendency traced over time) versus status (a settled condition to avoid inheriting): the difference marks whether the text is charting a pattern or defining a state.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'rebel' (marah), read as an action (type 102). The bearer (105) is 'the prisoners', those who sat in darkness and irons, and the operation (106) is to rebel, its target (107) 'against the words of God'. The reading's coupling and locus fields carry each other's content (the coupling field holds 'external:god' and the locus field holds 'paired with spurning his counsel'); read together, the rebellion is Godward (116, external:god) and welded to their spurning of the Most High's counsel (112). No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse traces no cause but names the defiance as the reason for their chains - 'for they had rebelled'. No organ seats it (104 none). Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent) - though the passage narrates the outcome (bowed hearts, hard labor, none to help), the effect field itself is empty; the consequence is told in the surrounding verses, not marked as a dimension. The discovery (114) reads it as the defiance that earned the chains - affliction as the fruit of rebellion. Role is characteristic (115). Here rebellion is shown with its consequence trailing after it: the inner life rebels against God's words and is bowed down into darkness and irons. God, whose words are defied, is the arena; the reading exposes an interior whose revolt lands it in bondage.
narratives.story: The psalm describes people sitting in darkness, prisoners in misery and chains, and explains how they got there: they had rebelled against God's words and treated his counsel with contempt. Their defiance was an active thing, and it carried a cost - God bowed their hearts down with hard labor until they fell with no one to help. The rebellion and the spurning of his counsel were one movement, aimed straight at God. The psalm shows the consequence unfolding in the story that surrounds it, though it does not dwell on measuring it. What we see is an inner life whose revolt against God lands it in chains and darkness.
narratives.variation_note: One of five readings of H4784:rebell. Here (#5) marah is an action, bearer 'the prisoners', rebelling against the words of God and coupled with spurning his counsel - defiance shown with bondage as its fruit. It differs from #1 (5:10, enemies, volition) and from #2/#3/#4 in its companion pairing (spurning counsel, versus sinning in #2, grieving God in #3, forgetfulness in #4) and in that this verse also holds a second, distinct lexical (spurn, naats). The recurring verb is re-anchored each time to a new adjoining movement and, here, to a twin verb of contempt.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'spurn' (naats), read as an action (type 102): active contempt. The bearer (105) is 'the prisoners', and the operation (106) is to spurn, its target (107) 'the counsel of the Most High'. The reading's coupling and locus fields carry each other's content (the coupling field holds 'external:god' and the locus field holds 'paired with rebelling'); read together, the spurning is Godward (116, external:god) and welded to the rebelling (marah) of the same verse (112). Directive to preserve distinctions applies: this single verse holds two separate lexicals - rebelled (marah) refuses God's words, spurned (naats) holds his counsel in contempt; they are twins but not identical, one a refusal of the word, the other a disdain of the counsel, and the pairing is the finding. No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse traces no cause. No organ seats it (104 none). Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the contempt for God's counsel behind the imprisonment. Role is characteristic (115). The same naats used of the enemy reviling God's name (74:10) here names the prisoners' contempt for God's guidance; the inner life scorns the counsel meant to lead it, and the scorn helps earn its chains.
narratives.story: In the same breath that says these prisoners rebelled against God's words, the psalm adds that they spurned the counsel of the Most High - they treated his guidance with contempt. The psalm holds these two faults side by side without merging them: one is refusing God's word, the other is looking down on his counsel. Their scorn for the very guidance meant to lead them was part of what landed them in chains. The psalm does not explain where such contempt came from; it simply names it. What we see is an inner life that despises God's counsel and pays for it in bondage.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'forsake' (azab), read as an action (type 102). The bearer (105) is 'the wicked', and the operation (106) is to forsake the law, its target (107) 'God's word'. The coupling (112) is marked 'paired within its char-arc across the psalm' - a note that in Psalm 119 this lexical is one beat in a sustained thread rather than an isolated event. No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse does not trace what drives the wicked's abandonment of the law. No organ seats it (104 none): it is a whole-self defection, not organ-lodged. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the wicked's forsaking of the law that fires the psalmist's indignation - 'hot indignation seizes me because of the wicked, who forsake your law'. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is 'external:god'. The finding sits in the reaction: the wicked's abandonment of God's word is what provokes the psalmist's burning zeal. God's law is the arena; the reading exposes the wicked's defection as seen through the eyes of one whose own inner life burns against it.
narratives.story: The psalmist is seized by burning indignation - not for himself, but because of the wicked who abandon God's law. Their forsaking of God's word is an active defection, and within this long psalm it is one recurring note in a larger theme. The psalm does not explain what makes the wicked cast off the law; it simply shows their abandonment and the fire it lights in the psalmist. What we see is one defiant movement - people walking away from God's word - viewed through the heart of someone whose own inner life blazes against it.
narratives.variation_note: This item (H5800:forsak, azab) has two readings. Here (#2) the bearer is the wicked and the forsaking is an actual, present reality that fires the psalmist's indignation. In #1 (89:30) the bearer is David's covenant children and the forsaking is hypothetical - a conditional 'if they forsake my law' held within God's promise of enduring love. The difference is bearer (the wicked vs. covenant heirs) and mode (a real defiance provoking zeal vs. a projected possibility inside covenant fidelity).

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'forsake' (azab, negated), read as a disposition (type 102): here the characteristic appears as its refusal - a settled not-forsaking. The bearer (105) is 'the psalmist', and the operation (106) is to NOT forsake, its target (107) 'God's word'. The coupling (112) is marked 'paired within its char-arc across the psalm' - one beat in Psalm 119's sustained thread of fidelity. No source is recorded (103 absent): the verse does not trace the origin of his loyalty, only that it holds. No organ seats it (104 none): it is a whole-self fidelity, not organ-lodged. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as holding to the precepts though nearly destroyed - 'they had almost made an end of me on earth, but I have not forsaken your precepts'. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is 'external:god'. The finding is negative-space fidelity: pressed to the edge of death, the inner life refuses the very abandonment the family otherwise records. God's word is the arena the psalmist clings to; the same verb that names the wicked's defection here names its opposite - a loyalty that will not let go under mortal pressure.
narratives.story: Nearly destroyed by his persecutors, the psalmist makes a defiant claim of a different kind: even so, he has not forsaken God's precepts. Where others abandon God's word, he refuses to - and his refusal holds even when he has been pushed to the brink of death. This steadfastness runs like a thread through the whole psalm. It does not explain where his loyalty comes from; it simply shows it standing firm under the worst pressure. What we see is an inner life that, at the very edge of ruin, will not let go of God's word - the bright reverse of forsaking.
narratives.variation_note: This item (H5800:forsaken) has three readings. Here (#3) forsaking is a disposition and negated - the psalmist has NOT forsaken God's precepts despite near-destruction, a fidelity Godward. In #1 (22:1) it is an affect of being forsaken by God himself; in #2 (27:10) an affect of being forsaken by parents yet held by God. Across the three the same word turns from being forsaken (by God-felt, by parents) to refusing to forsake: bearer and direction invert, and here alone the movement is the psalmist's own steadfast loyalty.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be despised' (bazah), read as a state (type 102): a condition the self endures, not an act it performs. The bearer (105) is 'the psalmist', and the operation (106) is to be small and despised. The target (107) is 'none' (resolution none): the despising has no object the psalmist aims at - he is its recipient, not its agent, so no target is fitting. The coupling (112) is marked 'paired within its char-arc across the psalm' - one beat in Psalm 119's larger thread. No source is recorded (103 absent): though foes and the insolent surround him, the field names no cause; the lowly state simply stands. No organ seats it (104 none): it is a whole-self condition, not organ-lodged. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are unrecorded (109/110/111/113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the low, despised estate held with unbroken memory - 'I am small and despised, yet I do not forget your precepts'. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116). Distinct from the fathers' scorn of God's gift (maas, 106:24) and the enemy's contempt of God's name (naats, 74:10), this bazah is contempt received, not given: the inner life is the object of others' scorn, yet holds its grip on God's word unbroken. Others are the arena whose contempt presses; the finding is a small, despised self that does not let go of God.
narratives.story: The psalmist describes himself as small and despised - looked down on, treated as of no account - and yet, he says, he does not forget God's precepts. Here contempt is something he receives, not something he hands out; he is on the wrong end of others' scorn. The psalm does not say exactly who despises him or why; it simply lets the lowly condition stand. What matters is that even in this diminished, scorned state, his hold on God's word stays unbroken. What we see is a belittled inner life that refuses to loosen its grip on God.
